items.rationale: Control flow is the decision of which step runs next and when the process stops. Option a is the tempting error: data passed between steps is what flows, not who decides the order.

A workflow is a system where the developer's code picks each step, even if it calls the model several times. Option b is tempting because workflows often use several calls, but a call count does not decide it; who chooses the steps does.

items.answer: A system where the model directs its own process and chooses which tools to use, instead of following steps fixed in code.
accepted: the model decides the steps and tool use itself
the model owns the control flow
the model dynamically directs its own process and tool usage
a system where the model, not code, decides what happens next
items.rationale: An agent is a system where the model owns the control flow: it decides the next step, which tool to call and when to stop. Answering that an agent is any system with a tool or several calls misses that the point is who decides.

accepted: response time and cost per request
items.rationale: When the model decides its own steps, a request usually takes more model calls, so it is slower and costs more, and mistakes can compound. Naming accuracy as what rises is the tempting error; autonomy can help on open-ended tasks but does not improve accuracy automatically.

items.answer: Flexibility on open-ended tasks, where the steps cannot be listed in advance.
accepted: the ability to handle requests whose steps are not known in advance
the model's ability to choose its own steps
items.rationale: A fixed workflow trades flexibility for predictability, lower cost and lower latency, because code has fixed the steps. Answering accuracy is the tempting error: a fixed workflow is not less accurate on tasks whose steps are known.

Code fixes the first check and the early stop; once the model is given tools it may call in any order, it owns the flow, so control is split. Option b is tempting because code owns the first step, but the stem says the model chooses the order and number of tool calls.

Code fixed the order of all three stages, and the model only produces text and JSON inside them, so this is a workflow. Option c repeats the teammate's claim: a workflow can call a model many times, so the number of calls does not decide it.

The steps never change, so the fixed workflow (Design A) fits: 3 calls x $0.005 x 2,000 requests = $30 per month. An answer of $60 uses the agent's 6 calls, which is the design that does not fit a request with fixed steps.

The logged path never varies, so an agent would add calls without any decision to make; the fixed workflow gives the same result at lower cost. Option a is tempting because an agent's recovery can help reliability, but this path shows no failure or open decision to justify the higher cost.

items.answer: Request X can be run by code end to end; Request Y needs the model to own the flow after the first lookup, because its later lookups depend on what earlier results show, so the steps cannot be fixed in advance.
accepted: X by code, Y by the model, because Y's next step depends on earlier results
code for X because its steps are known; model for Y because the number and order of steps are not known beforehand
X is a fixed single lookup; Y is open-ended so the model decides
items.rationale: Request X has one known step, so code can own it; Request Y's next step depends on the previous result, so no fixed path fits and the model must direct it. The tempting error is giving both to the model, because both involve lookups, but X has nothing for a model to decide.
